decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has three short lessons. First, what being critical means: the mindset behind the word. Second, active versus passive engagement: what that mindset looks like when you read a source. Third, the language of criticality: the words that name each critical move. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the three lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
This short course is about being critical at university: what the word really means and how to do it. By the end you will be able to explain what being critical is, tell active engagement with a source from passive, and use the basic language of criticality - analysis, evaluation, synthesis and judgement.

These are not abstract study skills. 'Be more critical' is one of the most common things tutors write on student work, in every subject. Knowing what it asks, and having the habits and the words to do it, changes how you read, how you write, and the marks your work earns.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Three course outcomes framed up front: explain being critical, distinguish active from passive engagement, use the language of criticality.

practiceConnection.academic: Being critical is the habit academic work is built on. Every essay that asks you to discuss or evaluate, every seminar where views are weighed, every piece of reading you are expected to question rather than accept, draws on the same mindset. Build it now and it carries into every module of your degree, and into the judgement that professional work later asks of you.

grounding.note: W-OPEN states the three course outcomes and why they matter (AL-5)

decidedValue.whereNextBody: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the intermediate and advanced criticality courses take the mindset into evaluating interpretations, engaging with journal articles, and synthesising sources in your own writing. Going wider: the same habits underpin Academic Writing, Reflective Practice and Researching, where you put criticality to work on real tasks.
decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course. Being critical is no longer a vague instruction: it is a mindset you can describe and begin to use. You can explain what being critical means - a questioning, weighing habit rather than fault-finding or a switch. You can tell active engagement with a source from passive, and open up the discourse around what you read. And you have the language of criticality - analysis, evaluation, synthesis and judgement - to name each move. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

practiceConnection.academic: From here, being critical is something you practise in every module. Each time a brief says analyse or evaluate, each source you weigh rather than accept, each judgement you reach with reasons, is the mindset at work. It is also what professional life rewards: the ability to question, weigh evidence and decide with reasons travels well beyond your degree.

courseReferences.title: See pages 113 to 134 of Chapter 8, 'Critical thought and developing a critical edge in writing', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

items.stem: When a tutor writes 'be more critical' on your essay, what are they mainly asking for?
Which of these best shows the critical mindset rather than a passive one?
A student reads a source, accepts its claim, and writes it into their notes as a fact. This is an example of engaging with the source...
What does it mean to open up the discourse around a source?
Weighing how strong or well-supported a claim is, with reasons, is which move of criticality?
You draw three sources together into a view of your own that none of them stated alone. Which word names what you have done?
